title: Sample Size and Power — Intuition First, Calculation Second

hook.en: "How many patients do I need?" is the first question every student researcher asks and the one most often answered with "about 30". A study that is too small cannot find real effects, and the ones it does find tend to be exaggerated. Learn the logic before you touch a calculator.
hook.ur: "Mujhe kitne mareez chahiye?" har talib-e-ilm muhaqqiq ka pehla sawal hai aur jis ka jawab aksar "takreeban 30" hota hai. Bohat chhota study asal asar nahi dhoondh sakta, aur jo dhoondhta hai woh aksar barha-chara hota hai. Calculator chhune se pehle mantiq seekhein.

goal.en: By the end, you'll explain power in plain words, name the four things that decide sample size, perform a simple sample-size reasoning for a two-group trial, and know why "30 per group" is a poor rule.
goal.ur: End tak aap power ko saade alfaaz mein samjhayenge, sample size tay karne wali chaar cheezein batayenge, do-group trial ke liye saada sample-size mantiq karenge, aur jaanenge "30 per group" kyun kamzor qaida hai.

text.en: **Statistical power** is the chance that a study will detect a real effect of a given size. Researchers usually aim for **80 percent power**, with a **5 percent significance level**. Sample size depends on four things: the **effect size** you want to detect (smaller effects need more people), the **variability** of the outcome (noisier outcomes need more), the **power** you want and the **significance level**. Also allow for **drop-outs**. Halving the effect size needs about four times as many participants.
text.ur: **Statistical power** is baat ka imkaan hai ke study ek tay shuda size ka asal asar dhoondh le. Muhaqqiq aam taur par **80 fisad power** aur **5 fisad significance level** chahte hain. Sample size chaar cheezon par munhasir hai: **effect size** jo aap dhoondhna chahte hain (chhote asar ko zyada log), nateeje ki **variability** (zyada shor ko zyada log), aap ki chahi hui **power** aur **significance level**. **Drop-outs** ka bhi hisab rakhein. Effect size aadha karne se takreeban chaar guna zyada shirkat karne wale chahiye.

text.en: Think of **looking for a small coin in a dark room with a torch**. A weak torch (small sample) may miss it even though it is there. A brighter torch (larger sample) finds it more often. The smaller the coin (effect), the stronger the torch you need. Power is how bright your torch is.
text.ur: **Andheray kamray mein torch se chhota sikka dhoondhna** sochein. Kamzor torch (chhota sample) sikke ko chhod sakti hai chahe woh wahan ho. Tez torch (bara sample) zyada baar dhoondh leti hai. Sikka (asar) jitna chhota ho utni taqatwar torch chahiye. Power aap ki torch ki roshni hai.

title.en: Reasoning about sample size for a two-group trial
title.ur: Do-group trial ke liye sample size ki soch

steps.title: Decide the smallest effect worth finding
steps.detail: Use the minimal important change, for example 10 points on a 100-point pain scale. Do not choose the effect you hope for; choose the smallest that matters. || Sab se chhota asar tay karein jo dhoondhne ke qabil ho

steps.title: Estimate the variability
steps.detail: Find the standard deviation of your outcome in earlier studies or a small pilot, for example 20 points. || Variability ka andaaza lagayein

steps.title: Choose power and significance level
steps.detail: Usually 80 percent and 5 percent. For a very important question, choose 90 percent power. || Power aur significance level chunein

steps.title: Calculate with software and round up
steps.detail: Free tools such as G*Power or an online calculator give the number per group; here about 64 per group for a standardised effect of 0.5. Add 10 to 20 percent for drop-outs. || Software se hisab lagayein aur oopar round karein

steps.title: Report it honestly
steps.detail: State the assumptions in your protocol. If you cannot reach the number, say the study is a pilot and plan for estimation, not proof. || Imaandari se report karein

question.en: A small trial of 12 patients per group finds a large but non-significant effect. What is the best conclusion?
question.ur: 12 mareez per group ka chhota trial bara lekin ghair-significant asar paata hai. Behtareen nateeja kya hai?

feedback.en: Absence of significance is not absence of effect.
feedback.ur: Significance ka na hona asar ka na hona nahi.

text.en: The treatment definitely works, because the effect is large
text.ur: Ilaaj yaqeenan kaam karta hai, kyunke asar bara hai

feedback.en: A large effect in a small study may be chance.
feedback.ur: Chhote study mein bara asar ittifaq ho sakta hai.

text.en: The study was probably underpowered, so it is inconclusive rather than showing no effect
text.ur: Study shayad underpowered thi, isliye yeh asar na hona nahi balke ghair-faislakun hai

feedback.en: Yes — small studies often miss real effects.
feedback.ur: Haan — chhote studies aksar asal asar chhod dete hain.

question.en: If you want to detect an effect half as big, roughly how does the required sample size change?
question.ur: Agar aap aadhe size ka asar dhoondhna chahein to zaroori sample size takreeban kaise badalta hai?

feedback.en: Yes — sample size scales with the inverse square of the effect size.
feedback.ur: Haan — sample size effect size ke ulte murabba ke saath barhta hai.

feedback.en: Effect size is a main driver.
feedback.ur: Effect size ek bunyadi wajah hai.
Chhote asar ko zyada log chahiye.

question.en: Why is "30 per group" a poor rule?
question.ur: "30 per group" kamzor qaida kyun hai?

text.en: Because trials need at least 1,000 people
text.ur: Kyunke trials ko kam az kam 1,000 log chahiye

text.en: The needed number depends on the effect size, variability and power; 30 may be far too few or unnecessarily many
text.ur: Zaroori number effect size, variability aur power par munhasir hai; 30 bohat kam ya be-zaroorat zyada ho sakta hai

feedback.en: Yes — it is a calculation, not a custom.
feedback.ur: Haan — yeh hisab hai, riwaj nahi.

text.en: Because 30 is not a round number

**Choosing the sample size from convenience.** "We can only get 20 patients" is a reason to downgrade your question (a pilot or feasibility study), not to pretend a small study will prove something. Another trap is to compute sample size with the effect you hope for rather than the smallest effect that matters, which gives a number that is too small. Also, do not forget drop-outs.
text.ur: **Sample size sahulat se chunna.** "Hum sirf 20 mareez la sakte hain" aap ke sawal ko ghatane ki wajah hai (pilot ya feasibility study), yeh dikhawa karne ki nahi ke chhota study kuch sabit kar dega. Ek aur jaal sample size us asar se nikalna hai jis ki aap ummeed karte hain, sab se chhote ahem asar se nahi, jis se number bohat chhota aata hai. Drop-outs na bhoolein.

text.en: **Know what a small study can offer.** A clinic series of 15 patients can show feasibility, teach you about variability and generate ideas, even if it cannot prove effect. Use it to plan a larger study or to join a multicentre effort. Collaboration across clinics is often the best route to adequate sample size.
text.ur: **Jaanein chhota study kya de sakta hai.** 15 mareezon ka clinic series feasibility dikha sakta hai, variability ke baare mein sikha sakta hai aur khayalat paida kar sakta hai, chahe asar sabit na kar sake. Isay bare study ka plan banane ya multicentre koshish mein shamil hone ke liye istemal karein. Clinics ke beech taawun aksar kaafi sample size ka behtareen raasta hai.

question.en: Why do small studies often report exaggerated effects?
question.ur: Chhote studies aksar barha-chara asar kyun report karte hain?

answer.en: Small studies are noisy, so chance throws up both small and large estimates. Those that reach statistical significance are the ones with large estimates, and those are the ones that get published and noticed. This "winner's curse" means that significant results from small studies tend to be overestimates, and larger later trials usually find smaller effects.
answer.ur: Chhote studies shor wale hote hain, isliye ittifaq chhote aur bade dono andaaze paida karta hai. Jo statistical significance tak pohanchte hain woh bade andaaze wale hote hain, aur wohi shaya aur nazar mein aate hain. Is "winner's curse" ka matlab hai ke chhote studies ke significant nateeje barhe hue andaaze hote hain, aur baad ke bade trials aam taur par chhote asar paate hain.

beats.patient: A student plans a trial of a new exercise for neck pain. She expects a 20-point improvement but the smallest important change is 10, and the standard deviation is 20.
beats.assessment: A calculation based on 20 points would give about 17 per group; one based on the smallest important change of 10 points gives about 64 per group.
beats.treatment: She plans for 64 per group plus 15 percent for drop-outs (about 74 each) and decides whether she can reach it, perhaps with a second clinic.
beats.reassess: Her protocol states the assumptions, and a reviewer sees a credible plan.

text.en: **An under-powered study can mislead people into harm.** A small trial that fails to find a risk is not evidence of safety. A small study that finds a harmful effect should not be dismissed either. Treat safety signals seriously and look for larger data.
text.ur: **Underpowered study logon ko nuqsan ki taraf gumrah kar sakta hai.** Chhota trial jo khatra na dhoondh sake safety ka saboot nahi. Chhota study jo nuqsandeh asar paaye usay bhi radd nahi karna chahiye. Safety ke ishaaron ko seriyas lein aur bara data dhoondhein.

text.en: Button and colleagues showed that low statistical power is common in neuroscience studies, that low power reduces the chance of detecting true effects and also reduces the likelihood that a significant result reflects a true effect, and that small studies tend to overestimate effect sizes. Lenth's practical guidelines stress that sample size determination requires specifying a meaningful effect size and an estimate of variability, and that these inputs matter more than the formula.
text.ur: Button aur saathiyon ne dikhaya ke neuroscience studies mein kam statistical power aam hai, kam power asal asar dhoondhne ka imkaan kam karti hai aur is ka bhi ke significant nateeja asal asar ko zahir kare, aur chhote studies asar ke size ko barhane ka rujhan rakhte hain. Lenth ki amali rehnumai zor deti hai ke sample size tay karne ke liye ba-maani effect size aur variability ka andaaza batana zaroori hai, aur yeh inputs formula se zyada ahem hain.

text.en: **Effect, Noise, Power, Drop-outs.** Smallest effect that matters, the noise in the outcome, the power you want, and a margin for drop-outs.
text.ur: **Asar, Shor, Power, Drop-outs.** Sab se chhota ahem asar, nateeje mein shor, jo power chahiye, aur drop-outs ka margin.

summary.en: Power is the chance of detecting a real effect; sample size depends on effect size, variability, power and significance level.
summary.ur: Power asal asar dhoondhne ka imkaan hai; sample size effect size, variability, power aur significance level par munhasir hai.

summary.en: Use the smallest important effect, not the hoped-for one, and add a margin for drop-outs.
summary.ur: Sab se chhota ahem asar istemal karein, ummeed wala nahi, aur drop-outs ka margin jodein.

summary.en: Small studies are inconclusive and tend to overestimate effects; treat them as pilots.
summary.ur: Chhote studies ghair-faislakun hote hain aur asar ko barhane ka rujhan rakhte hain; unhein pilots samjhein.

front.ur: 80 fisad power ka matlab kya hai?

back.en: An 80 percent chance of detecting a real effect of the assumed size.
back.ur: Farz kiye gaye size ke asal asar ko dhoondhne ka 80 fisad imkaan.

front.en: What happens to sample size if the effect halves?
front.ur: Agar asar aadha ho jaye to sample size ko kya hota hai?

back.en: Significant results from small studies tend to be overestimates.
back.ur: Chhote studies ke significant nateeje barhe hue andaaze hote hain.

front.en: What should the target effect size be based on?
front.ur: Target effect size kis par mabni ho?

back.en: The smallest effect that matters to patients.
back.ur: Woh sab se chhota asar jo mareezon ke liye ahem ho.
